extracted.intended_audience: poets, writers, and readers of Horace seeking moral, stylistic, and practical advice
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from Horace's Satires and Epistles containing prescriptive remarks on behaviour, taste, moderation, and aspects of poetic conduct and craft. Useful for writers seeking classical guidance on style, originality, and moral disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Take off the signs and trappings of disease, Your leg-bands, tippets, furs, and muffatees...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dismiss exaggerated external signs and adopted trappings that proclaim a state (e.g., ‘madness’ or overwrought passion). Horace (through interlocutors) advises removing affected apparel/gestures when moved by sober wisdom — a general counsel against artificiality in manner and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not force reason onto inherently irrational subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: “If a thing is senseless, to bring sense To bear upon it is a mere pretence; Now love is such a thing...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a subject (love, passion, certain human behaviours) resists rational analysis; treating it as wholly rational is a pretence. In practice: choose forms and tones appropriate to the subject’s nature rather than imposing unsuitable logical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid childish or trivial behavior in serious matters
rubrics_metrics.description: “When you pick apple-pips, and try to hit The ceiling with them, are you sound of wit?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from small, frivolous antics when the situation demands dignity or seriousness. The passage condemns pointless games and trivialities as unbecoming — applicable to conduct and to the writer’s choice of focus/gesture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ape great men; avoid slavish imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: “You build, which means you try To ape great men, yourself some two feet high...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace criticizes attempts to imitate eminent figures merely to seem larger than one is. For writers: cultivate originality, avoid mere parroting of admired masters; imitation that distorts the imitator’s nature is unwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate verses to enhance the whole (add oil to feed the glow)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Now then, throw Your verses in, like oil to feed the glow.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inserted verses or polished lines to sustain and enrich the poem’s warmth and momentum. The metaphor recommends judicious additions that feed the work’s fire rather than gratuitous ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master combination of tastes (aesthetic/tactile sense of taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let no man fancy he knows how to dine Till he has learnt how taste and taste combine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True taste requires learning how elements interact. Applied to writing: learn how different stylistic elements combine (tone, diction, rhythm) rather than relying on isolated ‘tastes’ or fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to small practical details rather than mere ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: “'Tis gross to squander hundreds upon fish, Yet pen them cooked within too small a dish. So too it turns the stomach, if there sticks Dirt to the bowl wherein your wine you mix; ... Brooms, dish-cloths, saw-dust, what a mite they cost! Neglect them though, your reputation's lost.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace emphasizes that neglecting basic cleanliness or practical care undermines reputation even more than failing in luxurious display. For writers/editors: attend to fundamentals (clean copy, good presentation, basic craft) rather than only grand gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate moderation, contentment, and simple living
rubrics_metrics.description: “This used to be my wish: a bit of land, A house and garden with a spring at hand... Nor ask I more, kind Mercury, save that thou Wouldst give me still the goods thou giv'st me now”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace praises modest, self-sufficient living and warns against endless ambition. For creative practitioners: value a manageable, steady life that enables steady work and reflection rather than restless pursuit of status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent between professed ideals and daily conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: “You praise the life that people lived of old, When Rome was frugal and the age was gold, And yet, if on a sudden forced to dwell With men like those, you'd strenuously rebel...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace (via Davus) calls out those who espouse virtues but fail to live them. For authors: practice what you preach in theme and deed; inconsistency undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: True freedom is inner self-mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: “Who then is free? The sage, who keeps in check His baser self, who lives at his own beck, Whom neither poverty nor dungeon drear Nor death itself can ever put in fear...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom is defined as control of desires and passions. For the writer/artist: cultivate discipline and resistance to external pressures (fame, money, appetite) to maintain artistic autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-cultivation and reading refine character
rubrics_metrics.description: “You're bloated by ambition? take advice; Yon book will ease you if you read it thrice. ... Submit to culture patiently, you'll find Her charms can humanize the rudest mind.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace urges patience in self-improvement through study and culture: sustained reading and instruction will moderate faults. Practical implication: regular study of literature and philosophy improves taste and moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer virtue and honest dealing over the pursuit of rank or wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: “Gold counts for more than silver, all men hold: Why doubt that virtue counts for more than gold?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace counsels that while society prizes wealth, the superior aim is virtue and fair dealing. For creative workers: prioritize integrity of work and reputation over mere material success.
